## Introduction

In this seven-minute overview, we work out what a reader should cite
to find the materials behind a particular result. We connect a
GitHub release to an archived Zenodo record with a DOI, decide what
belongs in the archive, and briefly consider what to do when the data
cannot be shared.

A Git commit identifies a repository revision. A GitHub release gives
a tagged revision a name and a place for release notes and assets.
Zenodo can archive a copy of selected files and issue a DOI. An
archive makes the cited files available under the access conditions
of that record [@zenodo-reserve-doi].

## Releases on GitHub {#archiving-releases}

Allow about two minutes. A release marks the version of a project
that others should use or cite. In the workshop repository, preparing
a release follows the steps we have used throughout the session:

1.  Record the changes in `CHANGELOG.md` and commit that entry.
2.  Tag the commit and publish a release with notes on the
    [releases page](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/releases).
3.  Publishing the release triggers the workflows that build and push
    the RStudio and Binder images. With the Zenodo integration enabled
    for the repository, Zenodo also archives the tagged files.

For an analysis, one release ties together the pipeline script, the
report source, the lockfile, and the metadata at one tagged revision.
A reader can then retrieve that exact combination rather than the
repository's latest state.

## Inspect a Zenodo record

Allow about two minutes. Open the workshop's archived `v0.2.0`
release [@workshop-v020]. Find the creators, access conditions, and
the ZIP of that revision. Compare the Zenodo version DOI with the
GitHub release tag and the concept DOI in `CITATION.cff`. Cite the
version DOI for the files supporting a result. Cite the concept DOI
when referring to the evolving project.
[Version archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24357028) ·
[Concept DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24342489) ·
[GitHub release](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/releases/tag/v0.2.0)

The workshop has three connected locations:

| Resource | Role |
| --- | --- |
| [Workshop website](https://jbris.github.io/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/) | Read the published workshop materials. |
| [GitHub repository](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r) | Find the source files, history, and releases used to publish the site. |
| [Zenodo record 24357028](https://zenodo.org/records/24357028) | Find the archived `v0.2.0` release and its version DOI. |

The record's related identifier points to the repository's `v0.2.0`
tag. The live website can change as the project changes; cite the
archived version that supplied the files for a particular result.
Later archived releases have their own version records and DOIs,
connected through the concept DOI.

## Decide what to archive

Allow about two minutes. For the `HealthWellbeing` analysis, a
candidate list is:

-   The exact code revision, pipeline script, and Quarto report source.
-   The report and summary CSV, where upstream terms permit sharing.
-   The lockfile, actual environment record, and container image tag
    or digest if the run used a container.
-   The source citation, download URL, checksum, pin version and
    study inclusion rule, plus the codebook, dataset metadata, and
    reuse terms.

The upstream download is publicly accessible. Confirm its reuse terms
before including the raw file, pinned copies, or derivatives in a
deposit. If you cannot include a copy, document how an authorised
reader can obtain the source and recreate the selected input. A pin
version identifies an object in a particular board. Preserving the
version identifier with the checksum and filter lets another reader
understand what that object contained.

## When the data cannot be shared

Allow about one minute. Open science can include restricted-access
data: you can share the methods, code, metadata, and access
conditions while restricting the original observations.

Synthetic data generated with *synthpop* can help others test whether
a workflow runs. It does not let them verify findings computed from
inaccessible originals, and ordinary synthesis is not a privacy
guarantee. A differential privacy claim requires a validated mechanism
and privacy accounting [@near2021-synthetic-data]. The
[supplementary synthetic data exercise](10_synthetic_data.qmd) works
through an example after the workshop.

## Question for the room

Which DOI would you cite for the files behind a specific result, and
which single item would help a reader recreate the precise input?

## Checkpoint {#zenodo-checkpoint}

You can connect a cited archive to a specific release, distinguish
its DOI from a GitHub release tag, and list the files and metadata a
reader needs. You can explain how publishing a release produces a new
Zenodo archive. Use the archive's own citation for the record you
inspected and cite the original review separately for the study data.

We finish with questions and discussion.
[Questions and discussion](09_discussion.qmd)

## After the workshop: archive your own releases {#zenodo-github-integration}

To archive releases of your own repository, follow Zenodo's
[Enable a repository guide](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/github/enable-repository/):

1.  Connect your GitHub account to Zenodo if it is not already linked.
2.  In Zenodo's profile menu, select **GitHub**.
3.  Select **Sync now** to refresh the list of repositories.
4.  Find the repository you maintain and enable its slider.
5.  Refresh the page and check that the repository is enabled.

Once connected, publishing a new GitHub release triggers automatic
archiving in Zenodo. Inspect the resulting version record, its DOI,
metadata, and downloadable files after each release. The **Sync now**
control refreshes the repository list; published releases are the
events that create new archives.
